extraction.name: BoolQ
extraction.description: BoolQ is a reading comprehension dataset of 16,000 naturally occurring yes/no questions. Questions are paired with a passage from Wikipedia containing the answer, and annotated with a 'yes' or 'no' answer.
extraction.creator: Christopher Clark, Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Tom Kwiatkowski, Michael Collins, Kristina Toutanova
extraction.citeAs: Clark, C., Lee, K., Chang, M.-W., Kwiatkowski, T., Collins, M., & Toutanova, K. (2019). BoolQ: Exploring the Surprising Difficulty of Natural Yes/No Questions. arXiv preprint arXiv:1905.10044.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Questions were obtained from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine. Queries likely to be yes/no questions were heuristically selected, and retained if a Wikipedia page was returned in the top five search results. Human annotators then evaluated question quality, located an answer-bearing passage within the Wikipedia article, and annotated the answer. The dataset combines 13k questions from this pipeline with 3k yes/no questions from the Natural Questions training set.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: User-generated content data, Passive Data Collection
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Anonymized, aggregated search queries from the Google search engine, Wikipedia articles, and the Natural Questions training set.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Queries were filtered to identify yes/no questions by selecting queries where the first word belongs to an indicator set ('did', 'do', 'does', 'is', 'are', 'was', 'were', 'have', 'has', 'can', 'could', 'will', 'would') and are of sufficient length. Only questions where a Wikipedia page was among the top 5 search results were kept. Questions were paired with the specific passage selected by the annotator rather than the entire document.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators followed a three-step process: first, deciding whether a question is 'good' (comprehensible, unambiguous, and requesting factual information) before viewing the Wikipedia page; second, identifying a passage in the Wikipedia document containing enough information to answer the question (or marking it unanswerable); third, labeling whether the answer is 'yes' or 'no'.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: To evaluate quality, three authors labeled 110 randomly chosen examples and resolved disagreements by conferring to establish gold-standard labels. Answer annotations reached 90% accuracy against gold standards (out of disagreements, six were ambiguous/debatable and five were annotator misunderstandings). Because agreement was sufficiently high, single annotations were used for the full dataset.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset exhibits class imbalance, with 62.31% 'yes' answers in the training set. There is also a mild correlation between the nature of the question (topic and question type) and the likelihood of a 'yes' answer.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, validation, and testing of reading comprehension, question answering, and natural language inference models on natural yes/no questions (split into 9.4k train, 3.2k dev, and 3.2k test).
